item.title: In the image of their tools | Science
item.description: In the United States, spending on AI infrastructure now dwarfs investment in the Internet and railroads combined, but spending on the institutions that would let societies absorb that technology is, by comparison, negligible. This asymmetry creates a paradox. Models post striking benchmark scores while aggregate economic output barely moves: Economist Daron Acemoglu projects a total factor productivity gain of well under one percent over a decade, and firm-level studies find that task-level gains do not necessarily add up at the firm or economy level. This paradox follows from an institutional mismatch that can be addressed by reverse alignment, the deliberate redesign of institutions, norms, and skills, rather than of models, so that societies can absorb new forms of machine cognition.

item.title: Zero-sum mindsets and economic policy preferences | Science
item.description: When economists talk about inclusive growth or shared prosperity, they have in mind economic policies generating widespread gains across individuals in society. For example, economists since Adam Smith have argued there are potentially large gains to be had for society from fostering trading with others. However, for voters to support such ‘win-win’ policies partly depends on whether they perceive the world in zero-sum terms, where zero-sum thinking (ZST) is the belief that gains for an individual or group necessarily come at the expense of others. The idea originally stems from work by anthropologist George Foster, based on pre-industrial societies with scarce resources. However, work in psychology and economics has established that zero-sum mindsets are also relevant, perhaps increasingly so, for understanding preferences over economic policies in modern times in advanced economies. This has spurred work to understand the prevalence, nature, and malleability of zero-sum mindsets.

item.title: China’s farmland needs clean water drainage | Science
item.description: China is transforming its agricultural landscape by building 67 million hectares of high-standard farmland and is aiming to expand this area to 90 million hectares by 2030 (1). By improving irrigation, drainage, soils, and resilience to droughts and floods, the program has become central to China’s food security and climate adaptation. However, the rapid expansion overlooks the importance of clean agricultural drainage water. Before the completion of the planned farmland, China should ensure that the fields do not increase pollution in downstream waterbodies.
